claim: Cells in the hippocampus tuned to spatial location are called place cells.
source: Cells in the hippocampus tuned to spatial location (place cells) typically change their tuning when an animal changes context, a phenomenon known as remapping.
evidence: This is a definitional statement supported by established scientific knowledge in the field of neuroscience.

claim: Place cells typically change their tuning when an animal changes context.
source: Cells in the hippocampus tuned to spatial location (place cells) typically change their tuning when an animal changes context, a phenomenon known as remapping.
evidence: This is a well-established empirical observation in hippocampal research.

claim: The phenomenon of place cells changing their tuning when an animal changes context is known as remapping.
source: Cells in the hippocampus tuned to spatial location (place cells) typically change their tuning when an animal changes context, a phenomenon known as remapping.
evidence: This is a definitional statement establishing terminology.

claim: What counts as a 'context change' has never been precisely defined.
source: A fundamental challenge to understanding remapping is the fact that what counts as a ''context change'' has never been precisely defined.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field based on review of literature.

claim: Different remapping phenomena have been classified on the basis of how much the tuning changes after different types and degrees of context change.
source: Furthermore, different remapping phenomena have been classified on the basis of how much the tuning changes after different types and degrees of context change, but the relationship between these variables is not clear.
evidence: This describes existing classification schemes in the literature.

claim: The relationship between types of context change and extent of remapping is not clear.
source: Furthermore, different remapping phenomena have been classified on the basis of how much the tuning changes after different types and degrees of context change, but the relationship between these variables is not clear.
evidence: This is an assessment of ambiguity in the existing literature.

claim: Remapping can be formalized in terms of hidden state inference.
source: We address these ambiguities by formalizing remapping in terms of hidden state inference.
evidence: This is the central theoretical proposal of the paper.

claim: According to the hidden state inference view, remapping reflects subjective beliefs about the hidden state of the environment rather than objective, observable properties.
source: According to this view, remapping does not directly reflect objective, observable properties of the environment, but rather subjective beliefs about the hidden state of the environment.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the interpretation of remapping.

claim: The hidden state framework can resolve puzzles about the nature of remapping.
source: We show how the hidden state framework can resolve a number of puzzles about the nature of remapping.
evidence: This is a claim about the explanatory power of the proposed framework, demonstrated through simulations in the paper.

claim: Place cells fire when an animal occupies specific spatial locations called place fields.
source: Place cells of the hippocampus fire when an animal occupies specific spatial locations (place fields; O'Keefe, 1976).
evidence: This is supported by citation to foundational work by O'Keefe.

claim: The population of place cells collectively comprise a map of an environment.
source: Each place cell has its own respective place fields, so collectively the population of place cell comprise a map of an environment, in which each location corresponds to activity of a particular subset of place cells.
evidence: This is an established concept in hippocampal research.

claim: The hippocampus uses independent maps for each context.
source: The hippocampus is thought to use independent maps for each context.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation supported by empirical observations.

claim: Place field remapping involves the location of a place field changing or the place field disappearing entirely between contexts.
source: These independent maps can be observed through ''place field remapping'', in which the location of a place field may change or the place field may disappear entirely between contexts (Muller and Kubie, 1987; Colgin et al., 2008; Kubie et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: The sensitivity of place cells to context changes is consistent with studies implicating the hippocampus in context-dependent behavior.
source: The sensitivity of place cells to context changes is consistent with many other studies implicating the hippocampus in context-dependent behavior (Holland and Bouton, 1999; Gershman et al., 2010; Anagnostaras et al., 2001; Smith and Mizumori, 2006a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The precise relationship between context changes and remapping has remained elusive.
source: Despite its acknowledged importance, the precise relationship between context changes and remapping has remained elusive, due in part to ambiguity as to what counts as context change.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field.

claim: Researchers have operationalized context in many different ways including sensory cues, spatial location or geometry, and task.
source: Researchers have operationalized context in many different ways. For example, some researchers investigated the role of sensory cues (Knierim et al., 1998; O'Keefe and Conway, 1978; Muller and Kubie, 1987), whereas others investigated the effect of changing spatial location or geometry (Skaggs and McNaughton, 1998; Lever et al., 2002), or changing the task (O'Keefe and Speakman, 1987; Markus et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies using different operationalizations.

claim: Different experimental manipulations of context have produced different effects without cohering into a unified picture.
source: Not surprisingly, different effects have been observed for these different manipulations, without cohering into a unified picture of how context changes determine remapping.
evidence: This is an assessment based on review of the literature.

claim: The word 'context' is sometimes defined as experimenter-defined variables and sometimes as the animal's internal assessment.
source: Some of the confusion about what counts as a context change is due to inconsistent definitions of the word 'context'. Sometimes 'context' refers to experimenter-defined variables, such as physical location or sensory cues. In other cases, 'context' refers to the animal's internal assessment of the environment as indicated by neural activity or behavioral response.
evidence: This is an observation about inconsistent usage in the literature.

claim: In fear conditioning, animals preferentially freeze in the 'same' context as that in which they received shock, which doesn't necessarily have to be physically the same environment.
source: For example, in the fear conditioning literature, animals are assumed to preferentially freeze in the 'same' context as that in which they received the shock. This doesn't necessarily have to be physically the same environment, as long as the animal infers that it is the same environment (Chang and Liang, 2017; Gershman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies in fear conditioning.

claim: The relationship between observable properties of the environment and remapping is mediated by inferences about unobservable properties (hidden states).
source: Key to this account is the idea that the relationship between observable properties of the environment (including context) and remapping is mediated by inferences about unobservable properties of the environment (hidden states).
evidence: This is the central theoretical claim of the paper.

claim: Place fields remap when the animal believes it has entered a new hidden state.
source: According to this view (see also Fuhs and Touretzky, 2007; Gershman et al., 2014; Penny et al., 2013), place fields remap when the animal believes that it has entered a new hidden state.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations to related work.

claim: Remapping phenomena have been divided into several classes including global remapping, null remapping, partial remapping, and rate remapping.
source: Remapping phenomena have been divided into several classes (Colgin et al., 2008; Muller, 1996; Kubie et al., 2019). At the extremes, there is 'global' or 'complete' remapping (where no place fields are shared between contexts) and 'null' or 'lack of' remapping (where all place fields are shared between contexts). Between these extremes is 'partial remapping' (where some place fields are shared between contexts but some are not) and 'rate remapping' (where place fields are shared between contexts but have characteristically different firing rates).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review papers and empirical studies.

claim: None of the remapping categories can be regarded as strictly exclusive.
source: However, none of these categories can be regarded as strictly exclusive.
evidence: This is an inference based on review of the literature.

claim: Studies report correlations near zero between place fields in different contexts.
source: Although studies report correlations near zero between place fields in different contexts (Leutgeb et al., 2004; Muller and Kubie, 1987; Schlesiger et al., 2015), there are reasons to believe that correlations are not actually zero.
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Previous observations of global remapping might be artifacts of misalignment of maps between contexts.
source: A recent report suggests that previous observations of global remapping might be artifacts of misalignment of maps between contexts (Kinsky et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a recent study.

claim: Some place cells consistently encode reward across virtual reality contexts that otherwise express global remapping.
source: Some place cells have been found to consistently encode reward across virtual reality contexts that otherwise express 'global remapping' (Gauthier and Tank, 2018), so there is at least one class of place cells that have recently been found not to remap across contexts.
evidence: This is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: Many studies reporting global remapping report low but non-zero correlations.
source: More generally, many studies reporting global remapping report low but non-zero correlations (Leutgeb et al., 2004; Skaggs and McNaughton, 1998; Spiers et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple empirical studies.

claim: Studies reporting lack of remapping never report perfect place field overlap between contexts.
source: Conversely, studies reporting lack of remapping never report perfect place field overlap between contexts.
evidence: This is an observation based on review of the literature.

claim: Patterns of spatial firing show variability over time within a single context, as if more than a single map is used.
source: Indeed, even within a single context, patterns of spatial firing show variability over time, as if more than a single map is used in a given context (Fenton and Muller, 1998; Kay et al., 2019; Kelemen and Fenton, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: The extent of remapping for repeated presentations of the same context depends on the amount of experience the animal has had.
source: Additionally, the extent of remapping for repeated presentations of the same context depends on the amount of experience the animal has had (Law et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: Rate remapping is always accompanied by partial remapping.
source: Manipulations used to generate rate remapping do so for a fraction of the place cell population, while other cells in the population maintain or lose their place fields (Wood et al., 2000; Leutgeb et al., 2005a). In this way, rate remapping is always accompanied by partial remapping.
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies and logical inference.

claim: Protocols for generating rate remapping can produce a range of remapping states during learning, from no remapping to global remapping.
source: Additionally, protocols for generating rate remapping can sometimes produce a range of remapping states during learning, ranging from no remapping to global remapping. For example, Leutgeb et al., 2005a found rate remapping when comparing place field maps between circle and square enclosures. However, Lever et al., 2002 make the same comparison between circle and square enclosures, and find rate remapping as an intermediate state as the animal transitions from no remapping to global remapping over the course of learning.
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific empirical studies.

claim: Virtually all remapping is partial remapping.
source: The complications discussed above highlight the fact that virtually all remapping is partial remapping.
evidence: This is an inference based on the review of empirical findings.

claim: Place cell responses to manipulations are extremely heterogeneous.
source: Place cell responses to manipulations are extremely heterogeneous (Lee et al., 2004; Shapiro et al., 1997; Chen et al., 2013; Anderson and Jeffery, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple empirical studies.

claim: Remapping behavior can vary across animals.
source: Additionally, remapping behavior can vary across animals (Wills et al., 2005; Lever et al., 2002) as well as across laboratories (Guzowski et al., 2004; Wills et al., 2005; Leutgeb et al., 2005b; Colgin et al., 2010), see the ''Morph Experiments'' section of the Results for an in-depth exploration of one example).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple empirical studies.

claim: Heterogeneity in remapping arises from variability in beliefs across animals.
source: We will argue that this heterogeneity arises from variability in beliefs across animals.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim that will be supported by the model.

claim: Extinguishing an association after Pavlovian conditioning is not the same as unlearning it.
source: Since Pavlov, experimentalists have recognized that extinguishing an association after Pavlovian conditioning is not the same as unlearning it.
evidence: This is established knowledge in learning theory.

claim: Extinguished associations can return under various circumstances such as returning to the conditioning context or waiting a period of time.
source: The association can return under a variety of circumstances (Bouton, 2004), such as returning the animal to the conditioning context, or simply waiting a period of time before testing the animal.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review paper.

claim: Animals form a new memory during extinction which can compete with the conditioning memory at retrieval.
source: These phenomena seem to suggest that the animal is forming a new memory during extinction, which could compete with the conditioning memory at the time of retrieval.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation of empirical phenomena.

claim: Context serves as a particularly powerful retrieval cue.
source: Context, on this view, serves as a particularly powerful retrieval cue.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim based on learning theory.

claim: New memories are formed when an animal infers it has encountered an unfamiliar state, and old memories are updated when it infers it has encountered a familiar state.
source: One approach to these questions is to frame them in terms of hidden state inference (Gershman et al., 2010; Gershman et al., 2017a): new memories are formed when an animal has inferred that it has encountered an unfamiliar (previously unvisited) state, and old memories are updated when it has inferred that it has encountered a familiar state.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Bayesian inference offers a natural solution to the problem of determining when to form new memories versus update old ones.
source: As we formalize below, these inferences can be calculated using Bayes' rule, which computes a posterior probability distribution over hidden states by integrating prior beliefs about the hidden states with the likelihood of those hidden states given the animal's observations.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the computational framework.

claim: The state inference framework can explain many animal learning phenomena.
source: The state inference framework can naturally explain many animal learning phenomena (see Gershman et al., 2015), for a review).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review paper.

claim: A conditioned response takes longer to extinguish when reward is delivered probabilistically during acquisition (partial reinforcement extinction effect).
source: For example, a conditioned response takes longer to extinguish when reward is delivered probabilistically during the acquisition phase, a phenomenon known as the partial reinforcement extinction effect (e.g., Gibbon et al., 1980).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: According to the state inference framework, partial reinforcement renders the hidden state ambiguous, requiring more extinction trials to infer different states.
source: According to the state inference framework, partial reinforcement renders the hidden state ambiguous; it takes more extinction trials until the animal is confident that acquisition and extinction trials were generated by different states (Courville et al., 2006; Gershman and Blei, 2012a).
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation supported by citations.

claim: Each hippocampal map corresponds to a unique hidden state.
source: In this paper, we argue that the same framework can unify many different place field remapping phenomena, under the assumptions that (i) each map corresponds to a unique hidden state, and (ii) a map is activated in proportion to the posterior probability of the corresponding hidden state.
evidence: This is a theoretical assumption of the model.

claim: A map is activated in proportion to the posterior probability of the corresponding hidden state.
source: In this paper, we argue that the same framework can unify many different place field remapping phenomena, under the assumptions that (i) each map corresponds to a unique hidden state, and (ii) a map is activated in proportion to the posterior probability of the corresponding hidden state.
evidence: This is a theoretical assumption of the model.

claim: The current work is inspired by Fuhs and Touretzky, 2007.
source: A closely related idea was pursued by Fuhs and Touretzky, 2007, to which we owe the inspiration for the present work.
evidence: This acknowledges prior related work.

claim: The model stresses the role of uncertainty in hidden state inference and its connection with partial remapping, rate remapping, and population heterogeneity.
source: In particular, we stress the role of uncertainty in hidden state inference and its connection with partial remapping, rate remapping, and population heterogeneity.
evidence: This describes a key contribution of the current work.

claim: The model can explain the stabilization of place cell maps over time.
source: This connection allows us to explain phenomena such as the stabilization of place cell maps over time and the potential role of experience in place cell responses to morph enclosures, among other phenomena.
evidence: This is a claim about the explanatory power of the model, demonstrated in the Results section.

claim: The model can explain the role of experience in place cell responses to morph enclosures.
source: This connection allows us to explain phenomena such as the stabilization of place cell maps over time and the potential role of experience in place cell responses to morph enclosures, among other phenomena.
evidence: This is a claim about the explanatory power of the model, demonstrated in the Results section.

claim: As the animal collects more observations, the posterior tends to progressively concentrate on a single explanation.
source: As it collects more observations and thereby reduces its uncertainty, the posterior will tend to progressively concentrate on a single explanation of which observations come from which states.
evidence: This is a property of Bayesian inference with accumulating data.

claim: In the first study of remapping, removal of a subset of cues caused partial remapping without one-to-one correspondence between place fields and cues.
source: The first study of remapping O'Keefe and Conway, 1978 found that in an environment with four cues, some place fields disappeared with the removal of one or two cues, but most place fields maintained their firing with the removal of any two cues. In more modern terms, removal of a subset of cues caused partial remapping, but there was not a one-to-one correspondence between place fields and cues.
evidence: This is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: Remapping is in response to cue constellations rather than individual cues.
source: Thus, from the very beginning it was clear that remapping is not in response to cues but in response to cue constellations (see also Shapiro et al., 1997; Fenton et al., 2000; Muller and Kubie, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple empirical studies.

claim: Many place fields that rotated when a given stimulus was rotated still maintained their firing when that stimulus was removed.
source: Each of these studies involved separately rotating or removing groups of stimuli, finding that many place fields that rotated when a given stimuli was rotated still maintained their firing when that stimuli was removed.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from multiple studies.

claim: The place field map is responsive to cues but is not controlled by cues in a one-to-one fashion.
source: The significance of these results is that the place field map is responsive to cues but is not controlled by cues in a one-to-one fashion.
evidence: This is an inference from the empirical findings reviewed.

claim: The model posits that cues jointly inform the posterior over hidden states.
source: Viewing remapping as hidden state inference provides an important insight into this behavior. Our model posits that the cues jointly inform the posterior over hidden states.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim of the model.

claim: Individual cues typically exert only a weak effect on the posterior and hence on remapping.
source: Individual cues will typically only exert a weak effect on the posterior, and hence exert only a weak effect on remapping.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model.

claim: The model simulation shows that changing all cues leads to global remapping while changing a subset of cues leads to partial remapping.
source: The first probe is an observation where each feature has a value of 0 (no cues changed). The model prefers assigning the probe observation to the same hidden state as the previous observations, corresponding to no remapping. The second probe is an observation where the first feature has a value of 1 and the other features have a value of 0 (cue 1 changed). The third probe is an observation where the first and last features have a value of 1 and the other features have a value of 0 (cues 1 and 4 changed). For both of these, the model produces an evidence ratio near 0, registering a high level of uncertainty about the hidden state (i.e., partial remapping). The fourth probe is an observation where all four features have a value of 1 (all cues changed), for which the model prefers assigning the probe observation to a new hidden state, corresponding to global remapping.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 2.

claim: The model is sensitive to the configuration of cues with no one cue completely controlling remapping.
source: These simulations demonstrate how the model is sensitive to the configuration of cues; no one cue completely controls remapping, consistent with the experimental data reviewed above.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Partial remapping reflects inherent uncertainty about whether different observations are drawn from the same distribution.
source: From the perspective of our model, this 'partial remapping' reflects the inherent uncertainty about whether different observations are drawn from the same distribution.
evidence: This is a theoretical interpretation provided by the model.

claim: The relationship between environment shape and remapping depends on prior experience.
source: Initially, it was thought that different geometries necessarily corresponded to different maps (Muller and Kubie, 1987; Quirk et al., 1992) , but recordings had always been done in familiar environments. The first group to record throughout the course of learning found that there was no consistent relationship between environment shape and inferred hidden state (Lever et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: In Lever et al. 2002, place cells initially showed limited remapping between square and circle boxes, but after extensive experience they remapped between the two boxes.
source: In this experiment, place cells were recorded in rats who were alternately placed in square and circle boxes occupying the same location in the recording room day after day. Early in learning, there was limited remapping. Only after extensive experience in the two boxes did the animals remap between the two boxes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an empirical study and reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Sensitivity to context changes changes with experience.
source: This indicates that the sensitivity to context changes changes with experience.
evidence: This is an inference from the Lever et al. 2002 findings.

claim: Analogous experience-dependent remapping results have been found for other manipulations.
source: Analogous results have been found for the effects of experience on remapping in response to other manipulations (Bostock et al., 1991; Shapiro et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: The hidden state inference perspective explains that distinctions between hidden states are acquired gradually.
source: It is naturally explained by the hidden state inference perspective, which posits that uncertainty about hidden states evolves as more data are observed. In particular, distinctions between hidden states are acquired gradually, such that substantial remapping should only be observed after sufficient experience to counteract the ''simplicity bias'' favoring a small number of hidden states.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation provided by the model.

claim: The model simulation shows that early in training there is uncertainty about how many hidden states there are, whereas later two hidden states become more probable.
source: Early in training, there is uncertainty about how many hidden states there are (Figure 3C); the evidence provided by the observations is not yet sufficiently strong to overwhelm the simplicity bias of the prior. As more data are observed, the two-state hypothesis is eventually favored over the one-state hypothesis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Maps take time to stabilize, with repetition of a novel environment inducing less map similarity than repetitions of a familiar environment.
source: Maps take time to stabilize: repetition of a novel environment induces less map similarity than repetitions of a familiar environment (Frank et al., 2004; Leutgeb et al., 2004; Law et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: In Law et al. 2016, intra-environment map similarity increased as a function of experience.
source: In particular, Law et al., 2016 alternated presentation of two environments. They found that intra-environment map similarity went up as a function of experience (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an empirical study and reference to Figure 4A.

claim: The speed of LTP-induced place field formation is inconsistent with the slowness of map stabilization.
source: Long-term potentiation (LTP) had been tied to map stabilization (Kentros et al., 1998; Cobar et al., 2017), but the speed with which LTP can create place fields (single trials; Bittner et al., 2017) is inconsistent with the slowness of map stabilization.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparing findings from multiple cited studies.

claim: The hidden state inference model interprets map stabilization as the animal sharpening its representation of a state with more experience.
source: The hidden state inference perspective offers a different interpretation of map stabilization: as an animal gains more experience with a particular state, it sharpens its representation of that state (i.e., its uncertainty about the distributional statistics decreases), and consequently it becomes more confident in recognizing repetitions of that state.
evidence: This is a theoretical explanation provided by the model.

claim: The model simulation shows that early in training the one-state and two-state hypotheses have similar probabilities, whereas later one hidden state becomes overwhelmingly more probable.
source: Through the course of learning, the partition evidence ratio accumulates evidence in favor of the one-state hypothesis, corresponding to the emergence of a ''stable'' map. Indeed, early in learning, the animal does not know whether it is receiving observations from the simulation of Figure 3 or the simulation of Figure 4, as they are indistinguishable. Only after extensive experience is the animal able to identify which generative process is generating its observations.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Place fields can remap depending on internal variables such as movement direction or task.
source: For example, place fields can remap depending on internal variables such as movement direction or task (Smith and Mizumori, 2006b; Sanders et al., 2019; Wood et al., 2000; Muller et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Place fields tend to remap based on running direction on a linear track but not in an open field during random foraging.
source: In general, it is known that place fields can remap depending on which direction the animal is running on a linear track (Markus et al., 1995; Battaglia et al., 2004). However, place fields tend not to remap based on running direction in an open field.
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: Markus et al. 1995 found that remapping in response to movement direction was larger in directed foraging than in random foraging despite having the same sensory cues.
source: This is most clearly shown in Markus et al., 1995. They compared two conditions, both of which occurred in an open field: one in which the animal was randomly foraging, and one in which the animal was running between four specific locations in one of two directions. They found that the extent of remapping in response to movement direction was larger in the directed foraging condition than in the random foraging condition (Figure 5A) despite having the same sensory cues in the two conditions.
evidence: This is supported by citation to an empirical study and reference to Figure 5A.

claim: The model is more likely to infer two hidden states when given directional observations as opposed to uniform observations.
source: The model is more likely to put probability on the hypothesis that there are two hidden states when given the directional observations as opposed to the uniform observations. This is similar to the empirical results, where place fields are more likely to remap (more likely to infer two hidden states) when the animal is running in a directed fashion.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Cue rotation experiments report both extent of remapping and rotational angle of map orientation.
source: Experiments reported two types of changes in place field behavior in response to a given manipulation. One is extent of remapping, as we have been discussing in this paper. The other is which rotational angle the map is oriented towards.
evidence: This describes the types of measurements made in cue rotation experiments.

claim: The rotational offset in place fields frequently corresponds to the rotational offset observed in head direction cells.
source: This rotational offset frequently corresponds to the rotational offset observed in head direction cells simultaneously recorded from a variety of brain regions (Knierim et al., 1995; Hargreaves et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: When the cue card is rotated 180° while the animal is absent and the maze is cleaned, place fields retain their positions relative to the card and rotate 180° with respect to the room.
source: The animal is trained with a cue card consistently at 0° with respect to the minimally-cued room reference frame. The animal is removed from the maze, which is cleaned and the cue card is rotated 180°, before returning the animal. The finding is that place fields retain their positions relative to each other (no remapping) and relative to the card, so they rotate 180° with respect to the room reference frame (offset of 180°) (Rotenberg and Muller, 1997; Knierim et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: When the cue card is rotated 180° without removing the animal or cleaning the maze, place fields do not remap or rotate.
source: A similar experiment was performed where the cue card is rotated 180° without removing the animal or cleaning the maze. The finding is that the place fields did not remap or rotate in response to this manipulation (Rotenberg and Muller, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: The model simulation of the 180° dirty rotation shows the best offset is ~0° and the state evidence ratio favors the same hidden state but with more uncertainty than the clean rotation.
source: Our model finds that the best offset is −2° (Figure 6C, blue) and the state evidence ratio is in favor of assigning to the same hidden state (Figure 6B, blue). However, the evidence ratio is much closer to 0, which would predict a larger degree of heterogeneity in place field behavior than the earlier experiment, which is a comparison for which there was not sufficient empirical power (Rotenberg and Muller, 1997).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: When the cue card is rotated 45° in the animal's presence without cleaning, place fields do not remap and rotate by 45°.
source: What if the cue card was only moderately rotated in the animal's presence? Rotenberg and Muller, 1997 rotated the cue card by 45° in the animal's presence without cleaning the maze. They found that the place fields did not remap and rotated by 45°.
evidence: This is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: The model simulation of the 45° dirty rotation shows the best offset is 22° and the state evidence ratio favors the same hidden state.
source: We model this experiment the same way as the last experiment except that the test observation has 45° as its first entry. Our model finds that the best offset is 22° (Figure 6C, purple) and the state evidence ratio is in favor of assigning to the same hidden state (Figure 6B, purple).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figures 6B and 6C.

claim: Different labs have found different results with morph environments that are not directly comparable.
source: A persistent puzzle in the field is the inconsistent results from 'morph' environments that interpolate between different geometries (e.g., square and circle). Different labs have found different results with experimental setups that are not directly comparable (Wills et al., 2005; Leutgeb et al., 2005b; Colgin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: In 2005, two groups performed morph experiments with different results.
source: In 2005, two groups each performed an experiment to answer the question, 'How does the hippocampus represent a novel environment that is intermediate between two familiar environments?' Both groups familiarized rats in square and circle environments, and then tested them in intermediate environments (polygons with a variable number of sides). The two papers had different results (Figure 7A), characterized at the time in terms of whether the similarity curve had a discrete switch or a gradual switch.
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 7A which shows data from different studies.

claim: The major difference between Wills et al. 2005 and Leutgeb et al. 2005b was the extent of remapping between square and circle (complete vs. partial).
source: A much more striking point of comparison was the difference in the extent of remapping between the extreme square and circle environments. Complete remapping was observed between the square and circle in Wills et al., 2005, whereas partial remapping was observed in Leutgeb et al., 2005b. We believe that the findings of partial vs. complete remapping is the major difference in the findings of these papers, and is the one we focus on explaining.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of the two studies.

claim: Wills et al. 2005 used a training protocol designed for inducing complete remapping in 6 days and excluded animals that did not meet that criterion.
source: One is that they used different training protocols. Wills et al., 2005 used a training protocol designed for inducing complete remapping between square and circle in 6 days, and excluded animals that did not meet that criterion.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol from the cited study.

claim: Leutgeb et al. 2005b used similar training as Lever et al. 2002 for three weeks.
source: Leutgeb et al., 2005b used a similar training as Lever et al., 2002, see Figure 3) for three weeks.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol from the cited study.

claim: Wills et al. 2005 presented intermediate shapes in scrambled order whereas Leutgeb et al. 2005b presented them sequentially.
source: The second difference was that Wills et al., 2005 presented the intermediate shapes in a scrambled order on the test day, whereas Leutgeb et al., 2005b presented the intermediate shapes sequentially based on number of sides on the test day.
evidence: This describes differences in experimental protocols from the cited studies.

claim: A replication of Wills et al. 2005 using scrambled presentation resulted in limited remapping, demonstrating that scrambled presentation was not sufficient to force complete remapping.
source: The second difference (scrambled test order) was the focus of several theoretical explanations (Blumenfeld et al., 2006; Gershman et al., 2014), but a replication of Wills et al., 2005 using scrambled presentation resulted in limited remapping (Colgin et al., 2010), demonstrating that a scrambled presentation was not sufficient to force the hippocampus to use complete coherent remapping.
evidence: This is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: Colgin et al. 2010 attempted an exact replication of Wills et al. 2005 but got the opposite result.
source: However, the problem remains that Colgin et al., 2010 attempted an exact replication of Wills et al., 2005, but got the opposite result.
evidence: This is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: Animals in the Moser lab consistently progress through partial remapping to global remapping more slowly than in the O'Keefe lab.
source: We do not believe either lab's training to be inherently superior, but we do wish to point out that there are likely unreported idiosyncrasies of training that cause animals to consistently progress through partial remapping to global remapping more slowly in the Moser lab than in the O'Keefe lab (at least during the years 2000–2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of results across labs.

claim: Remapping behavior does not have a one-to-one mapping to experimenter-defined conditions.
source: The main implication of this is that remapping behavior does not have a one-to-one mapping to the experimenter-defined conditions; rather, remapping behavior responds to a huge array of experiential factors, and the experimenter is only aware of a subset of these factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the variability observed across studies.

claim: The model predicts that both sets of morph results can be observed in the same lab with the same protocol by presenting intermediate morph environments early or late in training.
source: We therefore predict that both sets of results can be observed in the same lab, with the same experimental protocol, simply by presenting the intermediate ''morph'' environments early or late in training.
evidence: This is a prediction of the model.

claim: The model simulation shows that the probability of assigning intermediate morph environments to the same hidden state as one of the extreme environments increases with the amount of training.
source: The probability of assigning intermediate ''morph'' environments to the same hidden state as one of the extreme environments increases with the amount of training.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the simulation results shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Partial remapping occurs when some fraction of place fields are perfectly retained and some fraction disappear or appear.
source: One option is that some fraction of the place fields are perfectly retained and some fraction disappear or appear. This would be called partial remapping.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about partial remapping.

claim: Rate remapping occurs when each place field modulates its peak firing rate.
source: Another possibility is that each place field modulates its peak firing rate. This would be called rate remapping.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about rate remapping.

claim: Both partial remapping and rate remapping coexist.
source: As mentioned in the Empirical Background section of the Introduction, both types coexist.
evidence: This refers back to empirical observations discussed earlier.

claim: The fraction of place fields that completely remap is correlated with the magnitude of rate remapping across different protocols.
source: One is that the fraction of place fields that completely remap seems to be correlated with the magnitude of rate remapping that is observed across different protocols. For example, the paper that coined the term 'rate remapping' (Leutgeb et al., 2005a) explores several different experimental manipulations. Rank ordering of their manipulations according to their measures of rate remapping (firing rate changes and population vector correlations) matches well with the rank ordering according to their measures of complete remapping (place field correlation and center of mass change).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an empirical study and analysis of their data.

claim: Increased uncertainty correlates with heterogeneity in remapping behavior across the population of place fields.
source: Another pattern that seems to occur in the literature is that increased uncertainty seems to correlate with heterogeneity in remapping behavior across the population of place fields.
evidence: This is an observation based on review of the literature.

claim: More heterogeneity was observed in Leutgeb et al. 2005b (partial remapping regime) compared to Wills et al. 2005 (global remapping regime).
source: One example of this pattern is the difference in heterogeneity observed between the protocol of Leutgeb et al., 2005b compared to that of Wills et al., 2005. More heterogeneity was observed in the experiment of Leutgeb et al., 2005b, who were in the partial remapping regime (red line in our Figure 7B), compared to the relatively coherent response observed across the population in the experiment of Wills et al., 2005, who were in the global remapping regime (blue line in our Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of cited studies and model simulations.

claim: Different animals respond differently to the same environments.
source: One challenge in the study of hippocampal remapping is that different animals respond differently to the same environments.
evidence: This is an observation about variability in experimental results.

claim: Many studies reported significant heterogeneity across animals in remapping behavior.
source: Indeed, many of the previously discussed studies reported significant heterogeneity across animals in remapping behavior.
evidence: This refers to observations from multiple cited studies.

claim: Different animals learn at differing rates in studies of remapping development.
source: Studies of the development of remapping over the course of learning frequently report that different animals learn at differing rates (Bostock et al., 1991; Lever et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical studies.

claim: In Wills et al. 2005, four out of six animals partitioned observations as expected, while two partitioned them differently and were excluded.
source: The pre-training for one of the morph experiments described above (Wills et al., 2005) had three different ways that the observations could be partitioned. Out of the six animals they trained, four animals partitioned the observations in the way the experimenters expected, and the other two animals partitioned the observations in the other two possible ways (and therefore were excluded from the rest of the study).
evidence: This is supported by citation to an empirical study.

claim: Variation in α was previously used to model age-dependent and individual variability in learning.
source: Variation in this parameter was previously used to model age-dependent (Gershman et al., 2010; Gershman et al., 2017b) and individual (Gershman and Hartley, 2015a) variability in learning.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior modeling work.

claim: The model predicts that an animal trained with higher variability in a feature will be more likely to assign a novel observation with a novel value in that feature to the same state.
source: The model predicts that an animal trained with higher variability in feature one will be more likely to assign the novel observation to the same state as the previous observations (i.e., not to remap; Figure 10B).
evidence: This is a prediction of the model demonstrated in Figure 10B.

claim: High variability makes place fields more 'tolerant' of deviations from the central tendency of the distribution.
source: Intuitively, high variability will make the place fields more ''tolerant'' of deviations from the central tendency of the distribution.
evidence: This is an intuitive explanation of the model's behavior.

claim: A similar result to the cue variability prediction was posted as a preprint by Plitt and Giocomo, 2019.
source: After initial submission of this paper, a similar result was posted as a preprint (Plitt and Giocomo, 2019).
evidence: This acknowledges related work.

claim: Hippocampal remapping provides a window into the process of hidden state inference.
source: We have proposed that hippocampal remapping provides a window into the process of hidden state inference.
evidence: This is the central theoretical claim of the paper.

claim: Animals receive a stream of observations which they attempt to partition according to hypothetical hidden states that generated them.
source: According to our framework, animals receive a stream of observations (data points), which they attempt to partition according to the hypothetical hidden states that generated them.
evidence: This describes the computational framework.

claim: Bayesian inference offers a natural solution to the problem of partitioning observations by hidden states.
source: Bayesian inference offers a natural solution to this problem.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the computational approach.

claim: The Bayesian nonparametric model used here has been previously invoked to explain other hippocampal-dependent behavioral phenomena.
source: The specific form of Bayesian nonparametric model that we employed here has been previously invoked to explain a number of other hippocampal-dependent behavioral phenomena (Gershman et al., 2010; Gershman et al., 2017a; Gershman et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The model recapitulates a broad range of remapping phenomena.
source: In this paper, we showed that this model recapitulates a broad range of remapping phenomena.
evidence: This is a summary claim about the model's explanatory power.

claim: Partial remapping corresponds to high levels of uncertainty about hidden state assignment.
source: Central to our account is the idea that remapping reflects inferences about the hidden state, and in particular that partial remapping corresponds to high levels of uncertainty.
evidence: This is a key theoretical claim of the model.

claim: Manipulations of sensory cues, environmental geometry, and training can be understood in terms of their effects on state uncertainty.
source: Manipulations of sensory cues, environmental geometry, and training can all be understood in terms of their effects on state uncertainty.
evidence: This is a summary of the model's explanatory framework.
